title: CREATIVE · AI as your creative partner

slides.name: 1 · AI as your creative partner

params.text: Using AI to amplify human creativity, not replace it

slides.notes:
AI AWARENESS DAY 2026 · Starter 3 · Principle: CREATIVE · 5 minutes

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
· Consider whether AI-assisted work is still 'yours'
· Understand what AI can and cannot contribute creatively
· Recognise that human creativity remains essential

FRAMING — from the teacher pack:
This connects directly to academic integrity, and different contexts have different rules (art vs. homework vs. professional work). Encourage students to develop their OWN skills, not just delegation skills.

There is no right answer to the main question. Do not manufacture one.

slides.name: 2 · Statement · frame

params.text: If AI helped you write a story or create artwork, is it still your creation?
Talk to the person next to you — 60 seconds

slides.notes:
This one genuinely splits a room, which is the point. Show the spread and let two people who voted differently argue it out.

Do NOT resolve it. The teacher pack is clear that this is contested ground; your job is to give them better tools for the argument, not to end it.

DISCUSSION PROMPTS
→ If AI helped you with an essay, is it still your work?
→ What unique perspective do YOU bring that AI cannot?
→ When should you disclose that AI helped with something?

options: Yes — if I did most of it

slides.name: 3 · Creative thinking is now one of the top five skills employers want

params.text: Creative thinking is now one of the top five skills employers want
Students using AI mainly to save time — freeing space for deeper creative work
Creativity and resilience — rising skills for 2030, WEF
Original ideas produced by AI — it recombines; it does not originate

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: WEF Future of Jobs Report 2025 · HEPI Survey 2025

slides.notes:
The third tile is the argumentative one and it is meant to be. If a student pushes back — "but it made something new" — that is a good two-minute detour: recombination at sufficient scale can look a lot like originality, and the difference is whether anything was meant.

The 51% is the hopeful number. Time saved is only valuable if it goes somewhere.

slides.name: 4 · So — is it yours?

params.text: It depends how you used it
And how much of YOUR creative input was involved.
Using AI for starting points is like using a dictionary.
An entire work with minimal editing is less clearly yours.
Can you explain and defend every creative choice in the work?

slides.notes:
Reveal one at a time.

Cards 4 and 5 are the two that students can actually carry into a homework decision at 11pm. Spend your time there.

If a student asks where inspiration ends and copying begins: inspiration transforms an idea through your own perspective and skill; copying reproduces it without adding anything. If you could swap the AI output for any similar output and nothing would be lost, it was never yours.

LAB — SlideForge shows 6 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: The other test — Would you be comfortable if your teacher knew exactly how AI was used?; What you provide — Vision, judgment, emotional truth, perspective, and the final decisions..

slides.name: 5 · Statement · frame

params.text: What do you bring that AI can't replicate?
Extension — if you have longer than five minutes

slides.notes:
HIDDEN BY DEFAULT — the teacher pack's sub-question.

A word cloud is the right shape for this: repeats grow, so the room watches its own consensus form in real time. It is also the single most affirming thirty seconds in the whole set of five starters — if you unhide one extension slide across the whole day, make it this one.

feedback.prompt: One word — what do you bring?

slides.name: 6 · What you bring

params.text: Your unique perspective, shaped by your life.
Genuine feelings that resonate with other people.
Knowing what's good, what works, and what matters.

slides.notes:
Extension — unhide together with the question before it.

LAB — SlideForge shows 6 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: Intentionality — Having a purpose and a message behind the work.; Ethical reasoning — Choosing what SHOULD be created, not just what can be..

slides.name: 7 · Two words worth knowing

params.text: AI that creates new content from patterns in training data — recombining existing patterns rather than having original ideas.
Being genuine and original: your own voice, experiences and creative choices, rather than delegating them.

slides.notes:
Both definitions were in the teacher pack only.

Useful counterweight if the room turns purist: tools have always been part of creativity — cameras, synthesisers, spell checkers. The question has never been whether you used a tool. It is whether the result means anything.

slides.name: 8 · Creative AI partnership

params.text: Five ways to keep the work yours
Generate ten ideas, then pick and improve the best one.
Let it handle the routine so you can make the real decisions.
Your experiences and perspectives are what make work original.
Think of AI as a starting point, not the finish line.
Always add your own judgment and personal touch.

slides.notes: Reveal one at a time. If you are short of time, end here.

params.text: The best creative work comes from human imagination enhanced by AI capability.

slides.name: 10 · Section · If any of this affected you

params.text: If any of this affected you
You will not be in trouble for asking for help.

slides.notes:
Say this out loud rather than leaving it on the slide.

Your tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead is available to help — name the actual person if you can.

From the teacher pack, the three messages that matter most:
· If you are targeted by deepfake abuse, it is NOT your fault.
· Creating AI-generated intimate images of anyone is illegal.
· You will NOT be in trouble for reporting — we are here to help.

Have the safeguarding details ready to share privately with anyone who comes to you afterwards.
